---
title: "How does a support vector machine draw the line?"
subtitle: "Two groups of points, one straight line, and a rule for choosing it that depends on almost none of the data."
engine: knitr
---

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="svm-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · every one of these lines separates the two classes · made-up points"}
:::

You have points that already carry a label, say loan applications marked approve or deny, and each one has two measurements. You want a rule for the next application, which arrives without a label. The simplest rule is a straight line: one side is approve, the other is deny.

The trouble is that there is rarely one such line. If the two groups can be separated at all, they can be separated in infinitely many ways, and each line would label a new point near the gap differently. You need a reason to prefer one.

## The widest street

The support vector machine breaks the tie with one idea. Of all the lines that separate the classes, take the one that stays as far as possible from the nearest point on either side. Picture the line as the centre of a street, and widen the street until it touches a point. The width of that street is the **margin**.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="svm-figure" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · the margin, and the points that hold it up"}
:::

The points the street touches are the **support vectors**. Move any other point, short of pushing it into the street, and the line does not change at all. The whole model is held up by a handful of observations, which is where the name comes from.

The line itself is written

$$\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is a point, $\mathbf{w}$ is a vector of weights and $b$ is an intercept. To classify a new point you plug it in and read the sign: positive is one class, negative is the other. The weight vector is perpendicular to the line, so changing $\mathbf{w}$ rotates the line and changing $b$ slides it sideways. [In more than two dimensions the line becomes a plane, then a hyperplane. The equation does not change.]{.side}

## The formula

Scale $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ so that the support vectors sit exactly at $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = \pm 1$. Then the width of the street is

$$\text{margin} = \frac{2}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}$$

so the widest street is the one with the smallest weights. That turns "find the best line" into a problem you can hand to an optimiser:

$$\min_{\mathbf{w},\, b} \; \tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + b) \ge 1 \;\text{ for every } i$$

Here $y_i$ is the label of point $i$, written as $+1$ or $-1$. Multiplying by it makes the left side positive whenever the point is on its own side, so the constraint says: every point on the correct side, and at least one unit clear of the line. The square and the half change nothing about the answer. They only make the calculus cleaner.

## Trading width for mistakes

Real classes overlap, and then no line satisfies every constraint. The soft-margin version lets a point break the rule by an amount $\xi_i$ and charges for it:

$$\min_{\mathbf{w},\, b} \; \tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C \sum_i \xi_i$$

A point with $\xi_i = 0$ is outside the street on its own side. Between 0 and 1 it is inside the street but still correctly classified. At 1 or more it is on the wrong side. The two terms pull against each other: a wider street, or fewer violations.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="svm-figure" data-step="2" data-steps="2:slide λ|3:move a point" data-caption="Fig. 3 · fitted live in your browser · made-up points"}
:::

The figure writes the same trade the other way round, as the course lectures do: $\sum_j \max\{0,\, 1 - y_j(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}_j + a_0)\} + \lambda \sum_i a_i^2$. There the knob $\lambda$ multiplies the margin term, so raising it widens the street and lets more points inside. [Exam trap: read the formula before the letter. On the error term, a large C means a narrow margin and overfitting risk. On the coefficient term, a large C or λ means a wide margin and underfitting risk.]{.side}

In R's `e1071` and `kernlab`, C sits on the error term, so it runs opposite to $\lambda$: a large C makes every violation expensive, the street narrows, and the model bends to fit the training points. A small C tolerates violations, the street widens, and the model is simpler. Neither end is right in general. You pick the value by cross-validation.

One practical rule comes before any of this. The method measures distances, so a variable recorded in large units will dominate one recorded in small units. Scale the features first.

## When a line will not do

Some data cannot be split by any straight line: a ring of one class around a cluster of the other, for example. The optimisation above only ever uses the data through dot products $\mathbf{x}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}_j$. Replace that dot product with a **kernel** function $K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ and you get the effect of mapping the points into a higher-dimensional space, where a flat separator exists, without ever computing the mapping.

| Kernel | Formula | When to use |
|:------:|:--------|:------------|
| Linear | $K = \mathbf{x}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}_j$ | The classes are roughly linearly separable |
| Polynomial | $K = (\mathbf{x}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}_j + 1)^d$ | Interaction effects between features |
| RBF (Gaussian) | $K = e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\|^2}$ | The default for nonlinear patterns |

## Run it yourself {.reference}

Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

Two clusters of labelled points, the starting position for everything above.

```{r}
#| label: plot-two-groups
#| fig-cap: "Two groups of points. Can you draw a line to separate them?"

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

# Two clusters
df <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(rnorm(30, 2, 0.6), rnorm(30, 5, 0.6)),
  x2 = c(rnorm(30, 2, 0.6), rnorm(30, 5, 0.6)),
  group = factor(rep(c("Deny", "Approve"), each = 30))
)

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1 (e.g., income)", y = "Feature 2 (e.g., credit score)")
```

Three lines that all separate them. Only one sits in the middle of the gap.

```{r}
#| label: plot-many-lines
#| fig-cap: "Many lines separate the data, but which one is best?"

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  # Bad line — too close to blue
  geom_abline(intercept = -0.5, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  # Bad line — too close to red
  geom_abline(intercept = 1.5, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  # Good line — right in the middle
  geom_abline(intercept = 0.5, slope = 1, linewidth = 1.2, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 5.5, label = "Too close to red", color = "gray40", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = 1.5, label = "Too close to blue", color = "gray40", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 4.2, label = "Best line", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2")
```

The sign of $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b$ tells you which side of the line a point is on.

```{r}
#| label: plot-sides-of-line
#| fig-cap: "Points on each side of the decision boundary get different signs"

# Show which side of the line each point falls on
w <- c(1, 1)  # weight vector
b <- -7       # bias

df$decision_value <- w[1] * df$x1 + w[2] * df$x2 + b
df$side <- ifelse(df$decision_value > 0, "Positive (+1)", "Negative (-1)")

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = side)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -b / w[2], slope = -w[1] / w[2], linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 5.5,
    label = "w · x + b < 0\n(Negative side)", color = "steelblue", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 1.5,
    label = "w · x + b > 0\n(Positive side)", color = "coral", size = 4) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2", color = "Side of boundary")
```

Change $\mathbf{w}$ and the line rotates.

```{r}
#| label: plot-w-rotates
#| fig-cap: "Different weight vectors rotate the decision boundary"

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.4) +
  # w = (1, 1): 45-degree line
  geom_abline(intercept = 7, slope = -1, linewidth = 1, color = "black") +
  # w = (2, 1): steeper
  geom_abline(intercept = 10, slope = -2, linewidth = 1, color = "purple", linetype = "dashed") +
  # w = (1, 2): shallower
  geom_abline(intercept = 5, slope = -0.5, linewidth = 1, color = "darkgreen", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 6.5, label = "w = (1,1)", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 6.5, label = "w = (2,1)", color = "purple", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 4.2, label = "w = (1,2)", color = "darkgreen", size = 3.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2")
```

Fit a real SVM with `e1071`, pull $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ back out, and circle the support vectors.

```{r}
#| label: plot-margin
#| fig-cap: "The margin is the gap between the boundary and the closest points (support vectors)"

library(e1071)

svm_fit <- svm(group ~ x1 + x2, data = df, kernel = "linear", cost = 1, scale = FALSE)

# Extract the weight vector and intercept from the SVM model
w_svm <- t(svm_fit$coefs) %*% svm_fit$SV
b_svm <- -svm_fit$rho

slope <- -w_svm[1] / w_svm[2]
intercept <- -b_svm / w_svm[2]
margin_offset <- 1 / w_svm[2]

sv_indices <- svm_fit$index

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  # Decision boundary
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Margin lines
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept + margin_offset, slope = slope,
              linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept - margin_offset, slope = slope,
              linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  # Circle support vectors
  geom_point(data = df[sv_indices, ], aes(x1, x2),
             color = "black", shape = 1, size = 6, stroke = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.2, y = 6, label = "MARGIN", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.2, y = 5.5,
           label = paste0("Support vectors: ", length(sv_indices)),
           size = 3.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2")
```

The constraint value for every point. The support vectors sit at 1; everything else is comfortably above it.

```{r}
#| label: plot-constraint-check
#| fig-cap: "The constraint value for each point — all must be ≥ 1"

# Compute y_i * (w · x_i + b) for each point
df$y <- ifelse(df$group == "Approve", 1, -1)
df$raw_score <- as.numeric(w_svm[1] * df$x1 + w_svm[2] * df$x2 + b_svm)
df$constraint <- df$y * df$raw_score
df$is_sv <- seq_len(nrow(df)) %in% sv_indices

ggplot(df, aes(x = seq_along(constraint), y = constraint,
              color = group, shape = is_sv)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), labels = c("Regular", "Support Vector")) +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 1.15, label = "Constraint boundary (≥ 1)",
           color = "red", size = 3.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Point index", y = expression(y[i] * (w %.% x[i] + b)),
       shape = "Type", color = "Class")
```

Overlapping data at three values of C. In `e1071`, C is on the error term, so a larger C gives a narrower margin.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cost-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Small C = wide margin (some errors OK). Large C = narrow margin (few errors tolerated)."

# Overlapping data
set.seed(99)
df2 <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(rnorm(50, 2, 1.2), rnorm(50, 4, 1.2)),
  x2 = c(rnorm(50, 2, 1.2), rnorm(50, 4, 1.2)),
  group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 50))
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (C in c(0.01, 1, 100)) {
  fit <- svm(group ~ x1 + x2, data = df2, kernel = "linear", cost = C, scale = FALSE)

  grid2 <- expand.grid(
    x1 = seq(-1, 7, length.out = 150),
    x2 = seq(-1, 7, length.out = 150)
  )
  grid2$pred <- predict(fit, grid2)

  plot(df2$x1, df2$x2,
    col = ifelse(df2$group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"),
    pch = 19, cex = 1.2,
    main = paste("C =", C),
    xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2"
  )

  points(grid2$x1, grid2$x2,
    col = ifelse(grid2$pred == "A",
      adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15),
      adjustcolor("coral", 0.15)),
    pch = 15, cex = 0.3
  )

  points(df2$x1[fit$index], df2$x2[fit$index],
    pch = 1, cex = 2.5, lwd = 2)

  legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
    legend = c(
      paste("SVs:", length(fit$index)),
      ifelse(C < 0.1, "Wide margin", ifelse(C > 10, "Narrow margin", "Balanced"))
    )
  )
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Data no straight line can separate.

```{r}
#| label: plot-nonlinear-data
#| fig-cap: "This data can't be separated by any straight line"

set.seed(7)
n <- 200
angle <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
r_inner <- rnorm(n / 2, 1.5, 0.3)
r_outer <- rnorm(n / 2, 4, 0.5)

df3 <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(r_inner * cos(angle[1:(n/2)]), r_outer * cos(angle[(n/2+1):n])),
  x2 = c(r_inner * sin(angle[1:(n/2)]), r_outer * sin(angle[(n/2+1):n])),
  group = factor(rep(c("Inner", "Outer"), each = n / 2))
)

ggplot(df3, aes(x1, x2, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2") +
  coord_equal()
```

The same data with a linear kernel and with an RBF kernel.

```{r}
#| label: plot-kernel-comparison
#| fig-cap: "RBF kernel draws a curved boundary where linear can't"

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

grid3 <- expand.grid(
  x1 = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 150),
  x2 = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 150)
)

# Linear kernel — fails
fit_lin <- svm(group ~ x1 + x2, data = df3, kernel = "linear", cost = 1)
grid3$pred_lin <- predict(fit_lin, grid3)

plot(df3$x1, df3$x2,
  col = ifelse(df3$group == "Inner", "coral", "steelblue"),
  pch = 19, main = "Linear Kernel (fails)", xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2")
points(grid3$x1, grid3$x2,
  col = ifelse(grid3$pred_lin == "Inner",
    adjustcolor("coral", 0.15), adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15)),
  pch = 15, cex = 0.3)

# RBF kernel — works
fit_rbf <- svm(group ~ x1 + x2, data = df3, kernel = "radial", cost = 1, gamma = 0.5)
grid3$pred_rbf <- predict(fit_rbf, grid3)

plot(df3$x1, df3$x2,
  col = ifelse(df3$group == "Inner", "coral", "steelblue"),
  pch = 19, main = "RBF Kernel (works)", xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2")
points(grid3$x1, grid3$x2,
  col = ifelse(grid3$pred_rbf == "Inner",
    adjustcolor("coral", 0.15), adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15)),
  pch = 15, cex = 0.3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## On one page {.reference}

```
THE SVM RECIPE
==============

1. GOAL: Find the boundary with the widest margin

2. FORMULA (soft margin):

   min  ½||w||²  +  C × Σξᵢ
        --------     --------
        "keep the    "penalize
         margin       errors"
         wide"

   subject to: yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 - ξᵢ

3. KEY PARAMETERS:
   C     → error tolerance  (tune via cross-validation)
   kernel → shape of boundary (linear, RBF, polynomial)
   γ     → RBF "reach"      (high γ = local, low γ = global)

4. SUPPORT VECTORS = points on the margin edge
   - Only these points define the boundary
   - More SVs = simpler/wider margin
   - Fewer SVs = tighter/narrower margin

5. ALWAYS SCALE YOUR FEATURES FIRST
   SVM uses distances — unscaled features with large ranges dominate
```

## Check yourself {.reference}

Before moving on, try to answer these without scrolling up:

1. What does the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ control geometrically?
2. Why do we minimize $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ instead of maximizing the margin directly?
3. What happens when you increase C? What about decreasing it?
4. Why are they called "support" vectors?
5. When would you use an RBF kernel instead of a linear one?
6. Why must you scale features before using SVM?
